title: "05-lists"
format: html
---

# Introduction

A **list** is a flexible R data structure that can contain multiple objects,
including objects of different types.

Unlike a vector, which normally contains values of the same basic type, a
list can contain:

- Numbers
- Character strings
- Logical values
- Vectors
- Matrices
- Other lists
- Data frames
- Functions
- Other R objects

For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


This list contains a character value, a numeric value, and a logical value.

> **Key idea:** A vector is usually homogeneous, while a list can contain
> heterogeneous objects.

# Creating a List

Use the `list()` function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_list <- list(
  10,
  "Hello",
  TRUE
)

my_list
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 10

[[2]]
[1] "Hello"

[[3]]
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


The three elements have different types.

Check the type:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
typeof(my_list)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "list"
```


:::
:::


The result is:

```text
list
```

# Named Lists

It is usually more useful to give list elements names.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


The names can be retrieved using:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "name"    "age"     "student"
```


:::
:::


# Accessing List Elements

There are three important ways to work with list elements:

```text
$
[ ]
[[ ]]
```

Understanding the difference between them is essential.

# Using `[[ ]]`

`[[ ]]` extracts the **actual element** from a list.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person[[1]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


Access by name:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["name"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


Access age:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["age"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 25
```


:::
:::


The returned object is the actual value.

For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
typeof(person[["age"]])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "double"
```


:::
:::


# Using `$`

The `$` operator is commonly used with named lists.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person$name
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
person$age
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 25
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
person$student
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


This is equivalent to:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["name"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["age"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 25
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["student"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


For named elements, these are usually interchangeable:

```r
person$name
person[["name"]]
```

> **Tip:** `$` is convenient and readable, while `[[ ]]` is more flexible
> when the element name is stored in another variable.

# Using `[ ]`

Single brackets select a **sublist**.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


Compare:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
person[[1]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


The first returns a list containing the first element.

The second returns the actual value.

This distinction is extremely important.

## Example


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


returns a list.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[[1]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


returns:

```text
"Sujan"
```

# `[ ]` vs `[[ ]]` vs `$`

Consider:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)
```
:::


| Syntax | Result |
|---|---|
| `person[1]` | A list containing the first element |
| `person[[1]]` | The first element |
| `person["name"]` | A list containing `name` |
| `person[["name"]]` | The value of `name` |
| `person$name` | The value of `name` |

A useful way to remember it:

```text
[ ]       → subset of a list
[[ ]]     → extract an element
$         → extract a named element
```

# Lists Can Contain Vectors

A list can contain vectors.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  scores = c(80, 90, 85)
)

student
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$scores
[1] 80 90 85
```


:::
:::


Access the vector:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student$scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80 90 85
```


:::
:::


Then access an individual score:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student$scores[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80
```


:::
:::


This combines two indexing operations:

```text
student
   ↓
$scores
   ↓
[1]
```

# Lists Can Contain Matrices

A list can contain a matrix.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data <- list(
  name = "Scores",
  matrix = matrix(
    1:6,
    nrow = 2,
    byrow = TRUE
  )
)

data
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Scores"

$matrix
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
```


:::
:::


Access the matrix:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data$matrix
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
```


:::
:::


Access an element of the matrix:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data$matrix[1, 2]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2
```


:::
:::


# Lists Can Contain Data Frames

Lists can also contain data frames.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student_data <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob"),
  score = c(85, 90)
)

student <- list(
  name = "Student Information",
  data = student_data
)

student$data
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   name score
1 Alice    85
2   Bob    90
```


:::
:::


# Nested Lists

Lists can contain other lists.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  contact = list(
    email = "example@email.com",
    phone = "123456789"
  )
)

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$contact
$contact$email
[1] "example@email.com"

$contact$phone
[1] "123456789"
```


:::
:::


Access the nested list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person$contact
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$email
[1] "example@email.com"

$phone
[1] "123456789"
```


:::
:::


Access the email:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person$contact$email
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "example@email.com"
```


:::
:::


Or:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["contact"]][["email"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "example@email.com"
```


:::
:::


Nested structures are common in real R objects.

# Length of a List

Use `length()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

length(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::
:::


This returns the number of top-level elements.

# Structure of a List

Use `str()` to inspect the structure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
str(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
List of 3
 $ name   : chr "Sujan"
 $ age    : num 25
 $ student: logi TRUE
```


:::
:::


`str()` is one of the most useful functions when working with complex R
objects.

For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  scores = c(80, 90, 85),
  passed = TRUE
)

str(student)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
List of 4
 $ name  : chr "Sujan"
 $ age   : num 25
 $ scores: num [1:3] 80 90 85
 $ passed: logi TRUE
```


:::
:::


It shows the names, types, and structure of the elements.

> **Tip:** When you receive an unfamiliar R object, try `str(object)` first.

# Modifying List Elements

You can modify an existing element.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

person$age <- 26

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 26
```


:::
:::


Modify using `[[ ]]`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["age"]] <- 27

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27
```


:::
:::


# Adding New Elements

You can add an element using `$`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person$country <- "Germany"

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27

$country
[1] "Germany"
```


:::
:::


Or:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person[["university"]] <- "TU Chemnitz"

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 27

$country
[1] "Germany"

$university
[1] "TU Chemnitz"
```


:::
:::


# Removing Elements

Assign `NULL` to remove a named list element.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  country = "Germany"
)

person$country <- NULL

person
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25
```


:::
:::


Check the result:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "name" "age" 
```


:::
:::


# Combining Lists

Use `c()` to combine lists.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
list1 <- list(
  name = "Alice",
  age = 23
)

list2 <- list(
  city = "Chemnitz",
  student = TRUE
)

combined <- c(list1, list2)

combined
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Alice"

$age
[1] 23

$city
[1] "Chemnitz"

$student
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


# Repeating Lists

Use `rep()` to repeat list elements.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

rep(x, times = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25
```


:::
:::


# Converting a List to a Vector

If all elements are compatible, a list can sometimes be simplified into a
vector.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(10, 20, 30)

unlist(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 10 20 30
```


:::
:::


Result:

```text
10 20 30
```

For a character list:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- list(
  "Alice",
  "Bob",
  "Charlie"
)

unlist(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Alice"   "Bob"     "Charlie"
```


:::
:::


> **Important:** `unlist()` removes the list structure and attempts to create
> a simpler vector.

# Named Lists and `unlist()`

Consider:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

unlist(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   name     age 
"Sujan"    "25" 
```


:::
:::


The result is a vector.

Because the vector must have a single basic type, R may perform type
coercion.

# Checking Whether an Object Is a List

Use:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
is.list(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


You can also use:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
typeof(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "list"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(person)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "list"
```


:::
:::


# Lists and Vectors

A vector normally contains values of one basic type:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
numbers <- c(10, 20, 30)

typeof(numbers)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "double"
```


:::
:::


A list can contain different types:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mixed <- list(
  10,
  "Hello",
  TRUE,
  c(1, 2, 3)
)

mixed
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 10

[[2]]
[1] "Hello"

[[3]]
[1] TRUE

[[4]]
[1] 1 2 3
```


:::
:::


Compare:

```text
Vector:
[10, 20, 30]

List:
[10, "Hello", TRUE, c(1, 2, 3)]
```

# Lists and Matrices

A matrix has a fixed two-dimensional structure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m <- matrix(
  1:6,
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

m
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
```


:::
:::


A list can contain multiple objects of completely different structures.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
objects <- list(
  numbers = c(1, 2, 3),
  matrix = m,
  text = "Hello",
  flag = TRUE
)

objects
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$numbers
[1] 1 2 3

$matrix
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

$text
[1] "Hello"

$flag
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


# Lists and Data Frames

A data frame is closely related to a list.

Each column of a data frame can have a different type.

For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob"),
  age = c(23, 25),
  passed = c(TRUE, TRUE)
)

df
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   name age passed
1 Alice  23   TRUE
2   Bob  25   TRUE
```


:::
:::


Conceptually, a data frame can be thought of as a collection of columns,
where each column has the same number of rows.

You can inspect its structure:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
str(df)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
'data.frame':	2 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ name  : chr  "Alice" "Bob"
 $ age   : num  23 25
 $ passed: logi  TRUE TRUE
```


:::
:::


This relationship between lists and data frames will become important in the
next chapter.

# List Indexing — Important Examples

Consider:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  scores = c(80, 90, 85),
  passed = TRUE
)
```
:::


## First element


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


Returns a list.

## First element's value


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student[[1]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


Returns the actual value.

## Name


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student$name
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


## Name using `[[ ]]`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student[["name"]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


## First score


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student$scores[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80
```


:::
:::


## All scores


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student$scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80 90 85
```


:::
:::


## Second score


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student[["scores"]][2]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 90
```


:::
:::


# Lists with Variables as Names

Suppose the element name is stored in a variable.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25
)

field <- "name"
```
:::


Using `$`:

```r
student$field
```

This looks for an element literally named `field`.

Instead, use `[[ ]]`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student[[field]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Sujan"
```


:::
:::


This retrieves the element whose name is stored in `field`.

> **Important:** `[[ ]]` is useful when the name or position is stored in a
> variable.

# Useful List Functions

## `names()`

Get or set names.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  "Sujan",
  25,
  TRUE
)

names(student) <- c(
  "name",
  "age",
  "student"
)

student
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


## `length()`

Get the number of top-level elements.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
length(student)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::
:::


## `str()`

Inspect the structure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
str(student)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
List of 3
 $ name   : chr "Sujan"
 $ age    : num 25
 $ student: logi TRUE
```


:::
:::


## `unlist()`

Convert a list into a simpler vector when possible.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
unlist(student)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   name     age student 
"Sujan"    "25"  "TRUE" 
```


:::
:::


## `is.list()`

Check whether an object is a list.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
is.list(student)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


# Applying Functions to Lists

R provides several functions for applying operations to list elements.

One of the most useful is `lapply()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
numbers <- list(
  c(1, 2, 3),
  c(4, 5, 6),
  c(7, 8, 9)
)

lapply(numbers, mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 2

[[2]]
[1] 5

[[3]]
[1] 8
```


:::
:::


This calculates the mean of each vector.

The result is another list.

# `sapply()`

`sapply()` is similar to `lapply()` but tries to simplify the result.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sapply(numbers, mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2 5 8
```


:::
:::


The result may be a vector instead of a list.

Compare:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lapply(numbers, mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
[1] 2

[[2]]
[1] 5

[[3]]
[1] 8
```


:::


# List Function Reference

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `list()` | Create a list |
| `length()` | Number of top-level elements |
| `names()` | Get or set element names |
| `str()` | Inspect structure |
| `is.list()` | Check whether object is a list |
| `unlist()` | Simplify list into vector |
| `c()` | Combine lists |
| `rep()` | Repeat a list |
| `lapply()` | Apply function and return list |
| `sapply()` | Apply function and simplify result |

# List Indexing Reference

Given:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
student <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  scores = c(80, 90, 85)
)
```
:::


| Operation | Code | Result |
|---|---|---|
| First element as list | `student[1]` | List |
| First element | `student[[1]]` | Value |
| Name | `student$name` | Value |
| Name with `[[ ]]` | `student[["name"]]` | Value |
| Scores | `student$scores` | Vector |
| First score | `student$scores[1]` | Value |
| Scores with `[[ ]]` | `student[["scores"]]` | Vector |
| Second score | `student[["scores"]][2]` | Value |

# Python Comparison

If you know Python, a basic R list is somewhat similar to a Python list:

| Operation | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Create | `list(1, "hello", TRUE)` | `[1, "hello", True]` |
| First element | `x[[1]]` | `x[0]` |
| Length | `length(x)` | `len(x)` |
| Add element | `x[[4]] <- value` | `x.append(value)` |
| Remove | `x[[2]] <- NULL` | `del x[1]` |

However, R's `$` and named-list behavior makes R lists particularly useful
for structured objects.

# Key Takeaways

- A list can contain objects of different types.
- Lists can contain vectors, matrices, data frames, and other lists.
- `list()` creates a list.
- `$` accesses a named element.
- `[[ ]]` extracts an individual element.
- `[ ]` returns a sublist.
- Understanding `[ ]`, `[[ ]]`, and `$` is essential when working with lists.
- Lists can be nested.
- `str()` is extremely useful for understanding complex objects.
- `unlist()` can simplify a list into a vector.
- `lapply()` applies a function to each list element and returns a list.
- Data frames are closely related to lists, which will become clearer in the
  next chapter.
